title: Arranging for the Lucky Strike Hit Parade
summary: Carter wrote weekly arrangements for the Lucky Strike orchestra, though he does not recall it as breaking a color bar.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working radio and television: network shows, studio staffs, talk-show bands

blocks.x: Right. But I think it was in

there, wasn't it, that you made arrangements for Mark [Wayno] (PHONETIC) and the Lucky Strike orchestra. At the time when you were closing at the Famous Door in early '42, and obviously before you had begun to tour.
Right. That was correct.
Because that was in that period, and that was a regular arrangement that you had to provide a fixed number of arrangements per week, I think.
Right. For the Lucky Strike Hit Parade.
Uh huh. Was that -- in your recollection at the time -- did that break some kind of color bar?
I don't know. I wasn't making a study of it at that time, and I don't remember who was doing what for whom. Well, in radio, I don't know ... I just don't remember.
Did you play with them and record at any time with Wayno?
I did record with him. I never played on the show with him. No.

But you made some records and you ... well, it was reported in April in Downbeat that somehow, in April of '42 that this was some sort of breaking of a color barrier in some way. You were playing in the

studios, you see, in the network studio -- even if it wasn't on a show. That was some achievement of some sort. You may not have realized it or thought about it at the time; maybe it wasn't -- but did you -- do you recall that this was something new for a black musician to record in a major studio?
Well, what do you mean, in a major studio? Was that in the A network studio that we recorded in? with Mark Warner? It wasn't for radio.
No, this was just purely for records.
Yes, yes.

So in that case, it talks about the network studio. I guess it means the same studio which broadcasts on the network, but this was not for the network. The microphones may have been the same, but this was a record that you were making, and not a record for broadcast, actually; I mean, not for broadcast on the Lucky Strike show.

Do you recall -- it says in 'DownBeat' that, actually, that before Warner took on some black musicians, they had never appeared in the studios -- in the broadcasting studios. Do you remember anything like that?
No, I don't remember that. I mean, after all, you've got to remember that prior to that time, Lionel Hampton and Teddy Wilson had been with Benny Goodman, and ...
Yes. Sure.
And I don't know about the network
studios, but I know that I recorded one time with Charlie Barnett's big band on trumpet in some studio downtown.

I think this is the case, as perhaps frequently happens, that journalists, jazz critics and historians are looking for firsts, looking for all kinds of sharp distinctions when something -- as we discussed earlier -- when something began, and when another thing began, and maybe it's a big exaggerated.
I don't remember. I know I didn't think of it as a breakthrough at the time.
